children: The rupee has begun September on a stronger footing, extending its winning streak against the US dollar. The Indian currency recently touched Rs 94.5 to a dollar, its fifth consecutive session of gains.

A stronger rupee may sound like a development that matters mainly to traders, banks and economists. But movements in the currency can also have a direct impact on household finances, from the cost of foreign travel and overseas education to returns on US investments, NRI remittances and even inflation.
So, what does a stronger rupee mean for your money?

One major reason is the large inflow of foreign currency through the RBI's special swap facility. FCNR(B) deposits have brought in $127.23 billion, while total inflows, including overseas borrowings, have reached $136.38 billion. Also, the dollar has weakened recently. The Dollar Index fell to around 99 after comments from US Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller reduced expectations of an immediate rate increase, according to experts.
Here are five ways the latest rupee movement can affect your money.
Foreign travel and overseas education could become cheaper

When the rupee gains value against the dollar, Indians who need to make payments in dollars can benefit. For instance, if you are planning a holiday in the US, a stronger rupee means you need slightly fewer rupees to buy the same amount of dollars. The same applies to Indians paying tuition fees or living expenses for children studying abroad. However, the benefit will depend on how long the rupee stays strong. A short-term move in the currency may not make a big difference to the overall cost of an overseas trip or education.

Amit Pabari, MD and CEO of CrForex Advisors, said, "The RBI's special swap facility has pulled in $127.23 billion through FCNR(B) deposits, and including overseas borrowings, total inflows now stand at $136.38 billion."

"Here's the twist. This window opened in June, and dollars have trickled in for nearly three months. Yet the rupee flexed its muscles only in the last week, once the scale of the number hit headlines and the market took notice. Better late than never, but the real question is what happens once this one-time boost fades, because the rest of the macro picture isn't cooperating as much," added Pabari.
Your US investments can be affected

A stronger rupee can be a mixed blessing for Indians who invest in US stocks, mutual funds or ETFs. Suppose you own a US investment worth $10,000. If the dollar is worth Rs 96, the investment is worth Rs 9.6 lakh in rupee terms.

If the rupee strengthens and the dollar falls to Rs 94.5, the same $10,000 is worth about Rs 9.45 lakh. This means the investment can lose value in rupee terms even if its price in the US market has not changed. That is why investors in overseas assets need to understand currency risk. Your return depends not only on how the investment performs but also on how the rupee moves against the foreign currency.
NRIs sending money home may get fewer rupees

A stronger rupee is not necessarily good news for everyone. For NRIs sending dollars to their families in India, a stronger rupee means the same dollar amount converts into fewer rupees. So, if the rupee continues to strengthen, families dependent on regular foreign remittances could receive slightly less in rupee terms. This is an important reminder that the same currency movement can help one household and hurt another.
Oil prices could eventually hit your household budget

Oil is one of the biggest risks for the rupee and, indirectly, for household finances. Crude oil has already moved above $91 a barrel, with prices rising more than 10 percent in a week amid renewed tensions around the Strait of Hormuz.

India imports a large part of its crude oil requirement. When oil becomes more expensive, Indian companies need more dollars to pay for imports. That can increase pressure on the rupee. The impact can eventually reach households through fuel prices, transport costs and the prices of goods that depend on transportation.

"If there's one factor that can quietly undo all the good cheer, it's oil. Tensions around the Strait of Hormuz have flared up again after nearly a month of calm, and crude has already climbed past $91 a barrel. Any fresh escalation could send prices marching towards the $100 to $104 zone, and that is not a comfortable thought for India," said Pabari.
Your overall cost of living can be affected

The rupee's exchange rate is closely linked to inflation because India imports several important products and raw materials. If the rupee weakens sharply, imported goods become more expensive in rupee terms. Higher oil prices can add to that pressure.

"India's Current Account Deficit has already widened to $4.2 billion, or 0.5 percent of GDP, for the April to June quarter, up from $3.4 billion, or 0.4 percent of GDP, a year ago. The merchandise trade deficit tells a similar story, swelling to $86.1 billion from $68.9 billion," said Pabari. For households, a weaker rupee combined with expensive oil can make it harder for inflation to come down.

title: Rupee rises to 94.5: 5 ways the currency move can affect your household finances
